subjects.name: Histology
lectureNames: Alimentary Canal: Esophagus to Large Intestine
Cellular Ultrastructure (TEM: Taste buds, Acini, Parietal cells)

questions.text: Examine this low-power histological section of the alimentary canal. Identify this organ:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, prominent muscularis mucosae, and submucosal tubuloacinar esophageal glands proper.
questions.keyConcept: Esophagus: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with submucosal esophageal glands proper.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of the small intestine. Identify this specific segment:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intestinal villi and crypts with pathognomonic submucosal branched Brunner's glands secreting alkaline bicarbonate-rich mucus.
questions.keyConcept: Duodenum: diagnostic submucosal Brunner's glands producing protective alkaline mucus.

questions.text: Examine this small intestinal histological section. Identify this segment:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Exceptionally tall, slender mucosal villi and prominent plicae circulares, lacking both submucosal Brunner's glands and aggregated Peyer's patches.
questions.keyConcept: Jejunum: tall, well-developed villi without Brunner's glands or prominent Peyer's patches.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of the distal small intestine. Identify the diagnostic lymphoid aggregates indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large aggregates of secondary lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches) occupying lamina propria and submucosa on the antimesenteric border.
questions.keyConcept: Ileum: hallmark aggregated lymphoid nodules (Peyer's patches) along the antimesenteric wall.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of the lower gastrointestinal tract. Identify this specimen:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Flat mucosal surface without villi, straight parallel crypts of Lieberkuhn densely lined by goblet cells, and outer longitudinal taeniae coli.
questions.keyConcept: Colon: absence of villi with straight parallel crypts densely populated by goblet cells.

questions.text: Examine this cross-section of a tubular gastrointestinal organ. Identify this specimen:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Narrow, irregular star-shaped lumen, absent villi, shallow crypts, and a complete confluent ring of prominent lymphoid follicles effacing the submucosa.
questions.keyConcept: Appendix: narrow stellate lumen with a circumferential ring of prominent lymphoid follicles.

questions.text: Examine this histological section from the dorsal lingual mucosa. Identify these pointed surface papillae:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pointed conical projections covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, serving a mechanical role and uniquely lacking taste buds.
questions.keyConcept: Filiform papillae: pointed keratinized projections providing mechanical friction, devoid of taste buds.

questions.text: Examine this sagittal histological section showing a mucocutaneous transition. Identify this organ:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: External hairy skin, intermediate vermilion red margin with high vascular papillae and translucent stratum corneum, and internal oral mucosa over orbicularis oris.
questions.keyConcept: Lip: transition from external hairy skin to translucent vermilion margin and internal oral mucosa.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of the gastric wall. Identify this specific anatomical region:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Shallow gastric pits (1/4 of mucosal thickness) and straight tubular glands densely packed with acidophilic parietal cells and basophilic chief cells.
questions.keyConcept: Gastric fundus/body: shallow pits with straight glands rich in parietal and chief cells.

questions.text: Examine this gastric histological section. Identify this specific anatomical region:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deep, branched gastric pits (extending 1/2 or more into mucosal depth) and branched, coiled tubular glands lined by pale mucus-secreting cells.
questions.keyConcept: Pylorus: deep branching gastric pits leading into coiled, mucus-secreting tubular glands.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of liver parenchyma. Identify this structural unit:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Hexagonal structural prism centered on a terminal central venule, with radiating hepatocyte plates separated by vascular sinusoids toward portal triads.
questions.keyConcept: Classical liver lobule: hexagonal structural unit centered on a terminal central venule.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of a hollow digestive organ wall. Identify this organ:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Highly folded mucosa lined by tall simple columnar epithelium with brush border, resting directly on a fibromuscular coat without muscularis mucosae or submucosa.
questions.keyConcept: Gallbladder: tall columnar epithelium with folded mucosa lacking muscularis mucosae and submucosa.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of a major salivary gland. Identify this gland:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Mixed seromucous gland with serous predominance (~80%), crescentic serous demilunes of Giannuzzi capping mucous acini, and prominent striated ducts.
questions.keyConcept: Submandibular gland: serous-predominant mixed acini with classic demilunes of Giannuzzi.

questions.text: Examine this histological section of a parenchymal digestive organ. Identify this organ:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Purely serous secretory acini with intra-acinar centroacinar cells, absence of striated ducts, and pale endocrine Islets of Langerhans.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreas: purely serous acini with centroacinar cells and endocrine Islets of Langerhans.

questions.text: In this high-resolution scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of the dorsal tongue, identify these surface papillae:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tapering conical, hook-like keratinized projections providing abrasive mechanical grip for food manipulation without taste receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Filiform papillae SEM: pointed mechanical projections forming an abrasive dorsal surface.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of an intraepithelial taste bud, identify the apical sensory opening:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Constricted apical mucosal opening through which microvilli of sensory gustatory cells contact dissolved chemical tastants.
questions.keyConcept: Taste pore: apical microvillar opening mediating chemical contact between tastants and gustatory receptors.

questions.text: Examine this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of a salivary secretory unit. Identify this structure:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Basally flattened heterochromatic nucleus compressed against basement membrane, with cytoplasm packed with electron-lucent mucinogen droplets.
questions.keyConcept: Mucous acinus TEM: basally flattened nucleus with electron-lucent, pale mucinogen droplets.

questions.text: Examine this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of a salivary acinar cell. Identify this cell:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Rounded euchromatic basal nucleus, extensive parallel stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum, and dense apical zymogen secretory granules.
questions.keyConcept: Serous acinus TEM: prominent basal rough ER stacks with apical electron-dense zymogen granules.

questions.text: Examine this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of a gastric epithelial cell. Identify this cell:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deep intracellular secretory canaliculi lined by microvilli, tubulovesicular membrane system, and abundant mitochondria supplying ATP for H+/K+ ATPase pumps.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal cell TEM: deep intracellular secretory canaliculi, tubulovesicles, and dense mitochondria.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of gut epithelium, identify this sensory endocrine cell:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Reaches the intestinal lumen via apical microvilli acting as chemoreceptors, with basal neuroendocrine granules directed toward lamina propria capillaries.
questions.keyConcept: Open enteroendocrine cell: apical sensory microvilli sampling luminal contents with basal secretory granules.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of intestinal epithelium, identify this basal endocrine cell:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Rests along the basal lamina without apical luminal contact, responding to mechanical stretch or paracrine cues, with basal secretory granules.
questions.keyConcept: Closed enteroendocrine cell: basally situated endocrine cell lacking direct apical luminal contact.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) between adjacent hepatocytes, identify this intercellular channel:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intercellular channel formed by plasma membranes of adjacent hepatocytes, lined by short microvilli and sealed by tight junctional complexes (zonulae occludentes).
questions.keyConcept: Bile canaliculus: intercellular bile channel sealed by tight junctions between adjacent hepatocytes.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of hepatic parenchyma, identify this perisinusoidal compartment:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Sub-endothelial gap between fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells and hepatocyte microvilli, containing fat- and vitamin A-storing Ito (hepatic stellate) cells.
questions.keyConcept: Space of Disse: perisinusoidal microvillar compartment containing vitamin A-storing Ito cells.

questions.text: In this scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of hepatic sinusoidal endothelium, identify these clustered fenestrations:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Grouped transcellular fenestrations lacking diaphragms organized into sieve plates, facilitating macromolecular exchange with the space of Disse.
questions.keyConcept: Sieve plates: clustered sinusoidal endothelial fenestrations facilitating macromolecular hepatic exchange.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of pancreatic tissue, identify these apical secretory organelles:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Round, electron-dense membrane-bound apical granules storing digestive proenzymes (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase) awaiting exocytosis.
questions.keyConcept: Zymogen granules: electron-dense apical secretory organelles storing proenzyme digestive cascades.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of the enterocyte apical pole, identify this specialized surface border:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense, parallel cylindrical microvilli anchored into the underlying actin-rich terminal web, multiplying absorptive surface area 20-fold.
questions.keyConcept: Striated border: dense parallel microvilli anchored to terminal web, dramatically increasing absorptive surface.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of intestinal epithelium, identify this mucus-secreting cell:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Polarized unicellular gland with narrow basal stem and expanded apical theca filled with electron-lucent mucinogen granules that lubricate the mucosa.
questions.keyConcept: Goblet cell: apical cup filled with mucinogen granules providing protective lubricating mucosal barrier.

questions.text: In this transmission electron micrograph (TEM) of an intestinal crypt base, identify these granule-filled cells:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pyramidal cells residing at the base of crypts of Lieberkuhn containing large, intensely electron-dense apical granules discharging lysozyme, defensins, and zinc.
questions.keyConcept: Paneth cells: crypt-base cells with prominent antimicrobial granules secreting lysozyme and defensins.

questions.text: This endoscopic biopsy from the distal esophagus of a patient with chronic reflux demonstrates epithelial replacement. What is the pathognomonic diagnostic finding?
options: Columnar intestinal metaplasia containing alcian blue-positive goblet cells
Severe squamous cell dysplasia with intact underlying basal membrane
Eosinophilic microabscesses without glandular or goblet cell conversion
Dense submucosal lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers
questions.explanation: Barrett esophagus is defined histologically by intestinal metaplasia where normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar cells containing true goblet cells, conferring risk for adenocarcinoma.
questions.keyConcept: Barrett esophagus: intestinal metaplasia with true goblet cells above GE junction.

questions.text: Examine this section from a benign parotid neoplasm (pleomorphic adenoma). What dual histological components define this mixed tumor?
options: Bilayered oncocytic columnar cells overlying dense lymphoid stroma
Solid sheets of poorly differentiated clear cells with vascular invasion
Sheets of mature signet ring cells filled with abundant intracellular mucin
Epithelial ductal structures embedded in myxoid and chondroid stroma
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma (mixed tumor) displays epithelial ductal structures and sheets intermingled with myxoid, chondroid, or fibrous mesenchymal-like stroma elaborated by neoplastic myoepithelial cells.
questions.keyConcept: Pleomorphic adenoma = epithelial ducts embedded in myxochondroid matrix.

questions.text: This photomicrograph demonstrates Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum). What microscopic architecture establishes the diagnosis?
options: Malignant stratified squamous islands surrounded by marked desmoplasia
Acellular laminated chitinous membranes with calcified brood capsules
Bilayered oncocytic epithelium lining cysts over lymphoid stroma with follicles
Mucin-secreting signet ring cells infiltrating the parotid gland capsule
questions.explanation: Warthin tumor consists of cystic spaces with papillary foldings lined by a uniform double layer of pink oncocytic columnar cells resting upon a dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.
questions.keyConcept: Warthin tumor: bilayered oncocytic epithelium + lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.

questions.text: This liver biopsy stained with Masson trichrome demonstrates blue-staining fibrous bands. What pathological triad defines liver cirrhosis?
options: Diffuse bridging fibrosis, architectural disruption, and regenerative nodules
Focal portal triaditis, central vein thrombosis, and preserved liver plates
Centrilobular macrovesicular steatosis without significant fibrous septation
Non-caseating granulomas with complete preservation of lobular architecture
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is defined pathologically by diffuse bridging fibrosis (blue on Masson trichrome), complete loss of normal lobular architecture, and parenchymal nodular regeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Cirrhosis triad: diffuse fibrosis + regenerative nodules + architectural disruption.

questions.text: A patient with cirrhosis develops a liver mass showing malignant hepatocytes. Which histological feature confirms hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
options: Orderly single-cell thick cords bordered by normal sinusoidal endothelial cells
Malignant glandular tubules producing abundant intracytoplasmic mucin
Small uniform round blue neuroendocrine cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin
Markedly thickened liver cell trabeculae (>3 cells thick) with atypical mitoses
questions.explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by loss of reticulin framework, markedly thickened trabeculae (>3 cells thick), pseudoacinar architecture, pleomorphic nuclei, and atypical mitoses.
questions.keyConcept: HCC: thick trabeculae (>3 cells), nuclear atypia, and loss of reticulin network.

questions.text: Examine this hepatic bilharziasis specimen (Symmers clay-pipe-stem fibrosis). What distinguishes schistosomal hepatic fibrosis from true cirrhosis?
options: Widespread hepatocellular necrosis with diffuse micro-nodular regeneration
Preservation of normal lobular architecture and absence of regenerative nodules
Severe diffuse macrovesicular fatty change affecting all lobular zones
Primary obliteration of major hepatic veins with centrilobular congestion
questions.explanation: In Symmers clay-pipe-stem fibrosis, granulomatous and dense fibrosis is restricted to periportal spaces, while lobular architecture and central veins are preserved without regenerative nodules.
questions.keyConcept: Symmers fibrosis: periportal fibrosis with preserved lobular architecture (non-cirrhotic).

title: Practical — Parasitology
subtitle: Helminths, Protozoa, Vectors, Eggs & Clinical Stations

subjects.name: Parasitology
lectureNames: Adult Flukes & Nematodes (Fasciola, Trichuris, Schistosoma, Enterobius)
Snail Intermediate Hosts & Diagnostic Helminth Eggs
Clinical Spotter Stations: Hydatid, Strongyloides & Schistosoma
Clinical Spotter Stations: Giardia, Fasciola, Enterobius & Hookworm

questions.text: Examine this whole-mount microscopic slide of an adult trematode. Identify this parasite:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large flat leaf-like body (20–30 mm) with distinct anterior cone and wide shoulders; intestinal ceca with extensive lateral and medial branching; dendritic tandem testes; habitat in hepatic bile ducts.
questions.keyConcept: Fasciola hepatica adult: cephalic cone, distinct shoulders, highly branched ceca and dendritic testes.

questions.text: Examine this adult nematode specimen. Identify this parasite:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Whip-like shape with thin capillary anterior 3/5 (containing stichosome esophagus) and stout posterior 2/5 housing reproductive organs; male posterior is coiled 360 degrees with a single spicule; habitat in cecum.
questions.keyConcept: Trichuris trichiura adult: whip-like body with attenuated anterior 3/5 (stichosome) and stout posterior 2/5.

questions.text: Examine this dioecious blood fluke slide. Identify these adult parasites:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dioecious trematodes; male is stout (6–12 mm) with dorsal tuberculations and ventral gynaecophoric canal; female is slender, cylindrical (7–17 mm) carried within the canal; habitat in mesenteric venules.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma mansoni adults: tuberculated male with ventral gynaecophoric canal enclosing slender female.

questions.text: Examine this adult female roundworm specimen. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small white spindle-shaped worm (8–13 mm); lateral cuticular cephalic alae; characteristic muscular double-bulb esophagus; long, straight, pointed pin-like tail forming 1/3 of body length; habitat in cecum/perianal.
questions.keyConcept: Enterobius vermicularis female: cephalic alae, double-bulb esophagus, and sharp pointed pin-like tail.

questions.text: Examine this minute adult tapeworm (3-6 mm). Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Minute cyclophyllidean cestode (3–6 mm); scolex with 4 suckers and rostellum with double row of hooks; strobila contains only 3–4 proglottids, terminal gravid proglottid exceeds half the worm length; habitat in canine small bowel.
questions.keyConcept: Echinococcus granulosus adult: tiny 3–4 segmented tapeworm with armed scolex and massive gravid proglottid.

questions.text: Examine this minute pear-shaped intestinal fluke (1-1.7 mm). Identify this parasite:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Minute pyriform body (1.0–1.7 mm); scaly spine-bearing cuticle; three suckers: oral, ventral, and a sublateral genital sucker (gonotyl) bearing 70–80 chitinous teeth; two oval testes at posterior end; habitat in small intestine.
questions.keyConcept: Heterophyes heterophyes adult: minute pear-shaped fluke with three suckers including a rodlet-armed gonotyl.

questions.text: In this high-power micrograph of a hookworm buccal capsule, identify the genus shown:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Heavily chitinized oval buccal capsule bearing two pairs of curved ventral teeth on upper border (vs. semilunar cutting plates in Necator); male copulatory bursa supported by tripartite dorsal ray; habitat in duodenum/jejunum.
questions.keyConcept: Ancylostoma duodenale buccal capsule: two pairs of sharp, curved ventral teeth on the anterior margin.

questions.text: Examine this microscopic parasitic female nematode. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Slender transparent nematode (2.2 mm); long cylindrical esophagus without bulb extending 1/3 of body length; divergent (amphidelphic) uterus containing a single row of 5–8 thin-shelled eggs; habitat in duodenal mucosa.
questions.keyConcept: Strongyloides stercoralis female: microscopic parthenogenetic nematode with long filariform esophagus.

questions.text: Examine this cestode scolex under the microscope. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Globular quadrate scolex (1 mm) with 4 hemispherical suckers and a rounded rostellum armed with a double crown of 22–32 hooks (armed scolex; vs. unarmed T. saginata lacking rostellum/hooks).
questions.keyConcept: Taenia solium scolex: quadrate armed scolex with 4 suckers and a double row of rostellar hooklets.

questions.text: Examine this tapeworm mature proglottid. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Transversely elongated proglottid (broader than long); centrally located dark rosette-like coiled uterus; central uterine pore (tocostome) discharging unembryonated operculated eggs; lateral follicular vitellaria.
questions.keyConcept: Diphyllobothrium latum mature segment: broader than long with a diagnostic central rosette-shaped uterus.

questions.text: Examine this stained gravid tapeworm proglottid. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Elongated rectangular proglottid (longer than broad); central uterine trunk with 15–30 main lateral branches on each side branching dichotomously (tree-like); actively motile, crawls out singly through anus.
questions.keyConcept: Taenia saginata gravid segment: 15–30 lateral main uterine branches per side branching dichotomously.

questions.text: Examine this larval trematode stage. Identify this cercaria:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Forked-tailed (furcocercus) cercaria; body has oral sucker, ventral acetabulum, and cephalic penetration glands; tail stem divides into two distal furcae; infective stage to humans via transcutaneous penetration.
questions.keyConcept: Furcocercus cercaria: forked-tailed cercaria of Schistosoma penetrating unbroken human skin in freshwater.

questions.text: Examine this larval cestode bladder worm. Identify this stage:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Oval translucent bladder (7–10 mm) containing fluid and an invaginated scolex with 4 suckers and NO rostellum or hooks (unarmed); larval stage of Taenia saginata in cattle striated muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Cysticercus bovis: unarmed larval cyst of Taenia saginata encysted in beef skeletal muscle.

questions.text: In this histological section of a cyst wall, identify the middle laminated layer indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Acellular, chitinous, refractile layer with parallel concentric striations (laminated membrane / ectocyst); secreted by the inner cellular germinal layer (endocyst); non-nucleated elastic supportive barrier.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatid ectocyst: thick, acellular, concentrically laminated cuticular membrane of Echinococcus granulosus.

questions.text: Examine this diagnostic larva passed in freshly voided stool. Identify this larva:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Length 200–250 um; short buccal cavity (shorter than head width); double-bulb rhabditiform esophagus; large conspicuous oval genital primordium at midbody (vs. hookworm larva which has long cavity, tiny primordium).
questions.keyConcept: Strongyloides rhabditiform larva: short buccal cavity with a large, prominent genital primordium in stool.

questions.text: In this appendiceal cross-section, identify these parasitic nematodes in the lumen:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Nematode cross-sections showing bilateral triangular cuticular alae projecting from lateral fields; meromyarian somatic muscle cells; gravid females packed with characteristic asymmetrical D-shaped eggs.
questions.keyConcept: Enterobius in appendix: distinct bilateral triangular lateral cuticular alae projecting into appendiceal lumen.

questions.text: In this colonic biopsy, identify these giant ciliated trophozoites:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Giant ciliate (50–100 um); surface pellicle lined by longitudinal rows of uniform cilia; anterior cytostome (cell mouth); large dense bean-shaped macronucleus with adjacent micronucleus; invasive in colon.
questions.keyConcept: Balantidium coli trophozoite: giant ciliated intestinal protozoan with a pathognomonic kidney-shaped macronucleus.

questions.text: In this fecal smear, identify this binucleated flagellated trophozoite:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Pyriform body (10–20 um) with bilateral symmetry; concave ventral sucking disk; two identical spherical nuclei with central karyosomes (face-like appearance); central axostyle; 8 flagella; falling-leaf motility.
questions.keyConcept: Giardia lamblia trophozoite: bilaterally symmetrical pear-shaped flagellate with two nuclei and ventral sucking disk.

questions.text: In this fresh stool dysenteric smear, identify the pathognomonic diagnostic feature:
options: Dense surface rows of longitudinal cilia
Phagocytosed red blood cells in cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Size 20–40 um; active directional monopodial pseudopodia; spherical nucleus with delicate peripheral chromatin and pinpoint central karyosome; pathognomonic presence of ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis).
questions.keyConcept: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite: pathognomonic erythrophagocytosis (ingested RBCs) confirming invasive amebiasis.

questions.text: In this Balantidium coli preparation, identify the prominent nuclear mass:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Balantidium coli possesses dimorphic nuclei: a massive somatic polyploid kidney/bean-shaped macronucleus governing vegetative metabolism, and a tiny diploid micronucleus tucked in its concavity.
questions.keyConcept: Balantidium macronucleus: large kidney/bean-shaped nuclear mass governing cellular vegetative metabolism.

questions.text: In this iodine-stained fecal mount, identify this quadranucleate cyst:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Oval shape (8–12 um) with distinct double-contoured wall; 4 spherical nuclei typically grouped at one pole; central longitudinal axostyle fibrils; curved claw-hammer shaped median bodies in cytoplasm.
questions.keyConcept: Giardia lamblia cyst: oval quadranucleate cyst with longitudinal axostyle and distinct double wall.

questions.text: In this fecal cyst comparison, identify the diagnostic features of Entamoeba histolytica:
options: Eight nuclei with eccentric karyosomes and splintered chromatoid bars
Single massive kidney-shaped nucleus with contractile vacuoles
Four nuclei with central karyosomes and smooth cigar-shaped chromatoid bars
Two nuclei with axostyle fibrils and polar claw-hammer bodies
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: E. histolytica mature cyst has 4 nuclei, central pinpoint karyosome, fine even peripheral chromatin, and thick chromatoid bars with rounded, blunt ends (vs. E. coli: 8 nuclei, eccentric karyosome, splintered bars).
questions.keyConcept: Entamoeba histolytica cyst: 4 nuclei with central pinpoint karyosomes and rounded cigar-shaped chromatoid bars.

questions.text: Examine this large spherical double-walled cyst. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large round to oval cyst (50–70 um); thick yellowish-green double wall; cytoplasm contains the persistent large kidney-shaped macronucleus, retracted cilia, and a contractile vacuole.
questions.keyConcept: Balantidium coli cyst: large 50–70 um spherical double-walled cyst with persistent bean-shaped macronucleus.

questions.text: In this modified acid-fast fecal smear, identify these bright-red oocysts:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small spherical oocysts (4–5 um); acid-fast positive (stain bright magenta-red against blue background); contain 4 slender naked sporozoites and a residual body; fully sporulated and infective when passed.
questions.keyConcept: Cryptosporidium parvum oocysts: 4–5 um acid-fast bright red spherical oocysts containing 4 sporozoites.

questions.text: Identify this freshwater molluscan shell vector:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Planorbid snail; shell coiled in a single horizontal plane (discoidal/flat-coiled); sinistral aperture; obligate intermediate host transmitting Schistosoma mansoni miracidia to furcocercous cercariae.
questions.keyConcept: Biomphalaria alexandrina: flat planorbid discoidal snail vector transmitting intestinal Schistosoma mansoni.

questions.text: In this comparison of operculated eggs, identify the giant egg shown:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Giant yellowish-brown operculated egg (130–150 um, largest in human stool); indistinct operculum at one pole; filled with unsegmented ovum and numerous yolk vitelline cells; unembryonated when laid.
questions.keyConcept: Fasciola hepatica egg: giant yellowish-brown operculated unsegmented egg (130–150 um).

questions.text: Examine this diagnostic egg in stool microscopy. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large oval egg (115–175 um); transparent golden shell; pathognomonic large sharp lateral spine pointing posteriorly; contains a fully formed ciliated miracidium; passed in feces.
questions.keyConcept: Schistosoma mansoni egg: large elongated oval egg with a pathognomonic prominent lateral spine.

questions.text: Examine this thin-shelled segmenting morula egg. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Elliptical shape (60 um); blunt rounded ends; extremely thin transparent shell appearing as a delicate black line; clear space between shell and 4–8 segmenting blastomeres (morula stage).
questions.keyConcept: Hookworm egg: extremely thin, transparent shell enclosing an internal 4–8 cell segmenting morula.

questions.text: In this comparison of spherical eggs, identify the radially striated egg:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Spherical shape (30–40 um); thick brown shell with diagnostic radial striations (embryophore); contains fully developed hexacanth embryo (oncosphere with 6 refractile hooklets); indistinguishable between T. solium and T. saginata.
questions.keyConcept: Taenia egg: thick brown shell with prominent radial striations enclosing a 6-hooked hexacanth embryo.

questions.text: Examine this barrel-shaped egg with bipolar plugs. Identify this species:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Barrel/lemon-shaped (50–54 um); golden-brown triple-layered shell; diagnostic clear transparent bipolar mucoid plugs protruding at both ends; contains unsegmented single-celled ovum.
questions.keyConcept: Trichuris trichiura egg: barrel-shaped golden egg with pathognomonic transparent bipolar mucoid plugs.

questions.text: Spotter examination: Identify this armed cestode scolex:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Armed scolex (1 mm) with 4 cup suckers and rostellum with 2 rows of hooks; distinguishing landmark from unarmed Taenia saginata which lacks rostellar hooks; ingestion of eggs causes human cysticercosis.
questions.keyConcept: Taenia solium scolex: 4 muscular suckers with a double crown of alternating chitinous rostellar hooks.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 1: A 42-year-old sheep farmer presents with right upper quadrant fullness. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a well-defined calcified unilocular hepatic cyst. Why is diagnostic needle aspiration contraindicated?
options: Risk of fatal anaphylactic shock and secondary intraperitoneal seeding
Impossibility of obtaining diagnostic hydatid fluid or hooklets
Certainty of causing acute severe portal venous thrombosis
Risk of triggering uncontrollable biliary fistulization
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Hydatid cyst of Echinococcus granulosus; puncture risks catastrophic spillage of highly antigenic hydatid fluid, provoking lethal IgE-mediated anaphylaxis and multiple secondary peritoneal hydatid implants.
questions.keyConcept: Hydatid cyst aspiration: strictly contraindicated due to risk of lethal anaphylactic shock and secondary seeding.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 2: A renal transplant recipient on high-dose corticosteroids develops paralytic ileus, severe diarrhea, and gram-negative sepsis. Stool reveals active rhabditiform larvae. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Massive exogenous reinfection through contaminated soil
Internal autoinfection leading to hyperinfection syndrome
Malignant transformation of dormant encysted larvae
Superinfection by swallowed adult Enterobius pinworms
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection; immunosuppression accelerates internal autoinfection where non-infective rhabditiform larvae rapidly molt into invasive filariform larvae within the bowel lumen.
questions.keyConcept: Strongyloides hyperinfection: internal autoinfection triggered by immunosuppression causing systemic larval dissemination.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 3: A 30-year-old farmer from the Nile Delta presents with hematemesis, splenomegaly, and ascites. Liver ultrasound shows Symmers' pipestem periportal fibrosis. Rectal biopsy shows eggs with large lateral spines. What is the etiology?
options: Direct occlusion of the main portal vein trunk by adult flukes
Toxic necrosis of hepatocytes caused by adult worm excreta
Granulomatous response to Schistosoma mansoni soluble egg antigens
Autoimmune destruction of interlobular intrahepatic bile ducts
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Schistosoma mansoni; eggs trapped in periportal venules release soluble egg antigens (SEA), stimulating CD4+ Th2 delayed-type hypersensitivity granulomas and periportal fibrosis without true cirrhosis.
questions.keyConcept: Symmers' pipestem fibrosis: granulomatous response to trapped Schistosoma mansoni lateral-spined eggs in portal tracts.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 4: A 6-year-old child presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension. Plain radiography demonstrates mechanical intestinal obstruction caused by a tangled mass of large roundworms. Identify the parasite:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Ascaris lumbricoides; largest human intestinal nematode (adults 15–35 cm); large worm burden tangles into a bolus causing mechanical small bowel obstruction, volvulus, or intussusception in children.
questions.keyConcept: Ascaris lumbricoides: giant intestinal roundworm capable of forming obstructive boluses in the ileocecal region.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 5: An AIDS patient with CD4 count of 45 cells/microliter suffers from relentless cholera-like watery diarrhea (10 L/day). Modified acid-fast staining of stool demonstrates 4-5 micrometer round pink oocysts. What is the cellular niche of this parasite?
options: Intracellular but extracytoplasmic at the enterocyte brush border
Obligate intranuclear replication inside lamina propria macrophages
Free extracellular swimming within the intestinal lumen fluid
Deep cytoplasmic residency in crypt-base Paneth secretory cells
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cryptosporidium parvum; resides within a parasitophorous vacuole at the apical enterocyte border: intracellular (enclosed by host membrane) but extracytoplasmic (outside host cytoplasm).
questions.keyConcept: Cryptosporidium cellular niche: intracellular but extracytoplasmic localization in enterocyte brush borders.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 6: A hiker develops foul-smelling, fatty, floating diarrhea (steatorrhea), flatulence, and epigastric cramping after drinking untreated stream water. Microscopic stool exam shows binucleate flagellated trophozoites. What causes the malabsorption?
options: Deep mucosal ulceration with transmural transmigration into blood
Mechanical coating and brush border flattening by ventral suction disks
Direct enterotoxin stimulation of cyclic AMP chloride secretion
Massive granulomatous destruction of mesenteric lacteal channels
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Giardia lamblia trophozoites adhere via ventral sucking disks to duodenal/jejunal microvilli, causing villous blunting, brush border enzyme deficiency, and fat malabsorption without mucosal invasion.
questions.keyConcept: Giardia malabsorption: mechanical mucosal adherence via suction disks causing diffuse brush-border impairment.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 7: A 38-year-old patient who routinely ingests raw wild watercress salad develops prolonged fever, tender hepatomegaly, marked eosinophilia (50%), and high serum transaminases. What was the infective stage ingested?
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fasciola hepatica / gigantica; human infection occurs by ingesting freshwater plants (watercress) harboring encysted metacercariae; juvenile flukes excyst in duodenum and migrate through liver capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Fasciola transmission: ingestion of encysted metacercariae on aquatic plants (watercress).

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 8: A 4-year-old child presents with intense nocturnal perianal pruritus and insomnia. A cellophane adhesive tape swab taken in the early morning demonstrates asymmetrical plano-convex eggs. Why is routine stool analysis usually negative?
options: Eggs dissolve rapidly in alkaline intestinal fecal secretions
Gravid females migrate out of the anus to oviposit directly on perianal skin
Eggs are exclusively passed through the urinary bladder mucosa
The parasites reproduce exclusively via tissue asexual budding
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Enterobius vermicularis; gravid females migrate out through the anal sphincter at night and oviposit in the perianal folds rather than in the stool stream; diagnosis is made via Scotch tape perianal swab.
questions.keyConcept: Enterobius diagnosis: perianal tape swab is required because females oviposit on perianal skin, not in feces.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 9: A 45-year-old traveler develops high swinging fever, right upper quadrant pain, and leukocytosis. Imaging reveals a solitary 8 cm hypoechoic abscess in the right liver lobe. Aspiration yields sterile anchovy-sauce-like fluid. Identify the causative agent:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica); trophozoites reach liver via portal vein from colonic ulcers, releasing pore-forming peptides (amebapores) and cysteine proteinases causing liquefactive anchovy-sauce necrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Amebic liver abscess: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites causing sterile liquefactive anchovy-paste liver necrosis.

questions.text: Clinical Case Station 10: A barefoot agricultural worker presents with severe pallor, exertional fatigue, and epigastric discomfort. Lab work reveals microcytic hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia (Hb 5.8 g/dL). Stool shows thin-shelled 4-8 cell segmenting eggs. What is the source of blood loss?
options: Chronic hemolysis caused by circulating parasite cytolytic toxins
Laceration of duodenal mucosa and active blood ingestion by adult worms
Autoimmune destruction of bone marrow erythroid progenitor cells
Splenic sequestration of red blood cells secondary to portal block
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Hookworm disease (Ancylostoma duodenale / Necator americanus); adult worms attach to duodenal mucosa with teeth/cutting plates, releasing anticoagulants and sucking blood (0.15–0.26 mL blood/worm/day).
questions.keyConcept: Hookworm anemia: mechanical duodenal mucosal laceration and active blood-sucking causing severe iron deficiency.

title: Practical — Anatomy
subtitle: Gross Specimens, Viscera, Vessels, Osteology & Cross Sections

subjects.name: Anatomy
lectureNames: Sagittal Head & Neck (Oral Cavity, Pharynx & Tonsillar Bed)
Retroperitoneal Great Vessels & Lumbar Plexus Topography
Blood Supply of Gut (Celiac Trunk, SMA, IMA & Portal Vein)
Congenital Anomalies & Cross-Sectional Axial CT Anatomy

questions.text: In this sagittal section of the oral cavity and pharynx, identify the lymphoid structure in the tonsillar fossa:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Situated in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) and palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar).
questions.keyConcept: Palatine tonsil: lymphoid organ situated in the tonsillar fossa between palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

questions.text: In this deep dissection of the palatine tonsillar bed, identify the cranial nerve traversing the bed:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) courses along the lateral pharyngeal wall deep to the tonsillar bed, vulnerable to injury during tonsillectomy.
questions.keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve: traverses tonsillar bed supplying general sensation and taste to posterior 1/3 of tongue.

questions.text: On the dorsal surface of this dissected tongue, identify this V-shaped groove:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: V-shaped sulcus with apex at foramen cecum, demarcating the boundary between anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of the tongue.
questions.keyConcept: Sulcus terminalis: V-shaped groove separating oral and pharyngeal tongue segments.

questions.text: In this lateral head and neck dissection, identify the largest salivary gland shown:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Occupies the retromandibular fossa anterior to the mastoid process and sternocleidomastoid muscle, enclosed by deep investing fascia.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid gland: largest salivary gland situated in retromandibular space anterior to sternocleidomastoid.

questions.text: In this superficial facial dissection, identify the excretory duct crossing the masseter muscle:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from anterior border of parotid, crosses superficial to masseter, pierces buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.
questions.keyConcept: Parotid duct: traverses masseter and pierces buccinator to open opposite the upper second molar.

questions.text: In this submandibular triangle dissection, identify the artery grooving the submandibular gland:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Arises from external carotid, loops deep to digastric, grooves the posterior pole of submandibular gland, and enters face at anterior border of masseter.
questions.keyConcept: Facial artery: intimately grooves the posterosuperior aspect of the submandibular salivary gland.

questions.text: In this anterior abdominal wall dissection, identify the aponeurotic opening indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Triangular defect in external oblique aponeurosis located superolateral to pubic crest, transmitting spermatic cord or round ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Superficial inguinal ring: aponeurotic defect in external oblique through which the spermatic cord exits.

questions.text: In this anterior abdominal wall dissection, identify the conjoint aponeurotic insertion indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fused lower arching aponeurotic fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis inserting into pubic crest and pectineal line.
questions.keyConcept: Conjoint tendon: fused aponeurotic arch of internal oblique and transversus inserting into the pubis.

questions.text: On the posterior layer of the rectus sheath, identify this horizontal curved boundary:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Curved inferior margin of the posterior rectus sheath midway between umbilicus and pubic crest, below which all aponeuroses pass anteriorly.
questions.keyConcept: Arcuate line: inferior border of posterior rectus sheath where aponeuroses shift entirely anteriorly.

questions.text: In this posterior abdominal wall dissection, identify this large medial muscle:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Fleshy muscle arising from lumbar vertebral bodies, transverse processes, and discs, descending to insert on the lesser trochanter.
questions.keyConcept: Psoas major: medial posterior abdominal wall muscle arising from lumbar spine, housing lumbar plexus.

questions.text: On this posterior abdominal wall specimen, identify the vertebral level of the aortic bifurcation:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into common iliac arteries at L4, approximately 2–3 cm below the umbilicus, just superior to IVC confluence at L5.
questions.keyConcept: Aortic bifurcation: occurs at L4 vertebral level, slightly superior to IVC confluence at L5.

questions.text: In this lumbar plexus dissection, identify the nerve piercing the anterior belly of psoas major:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Only lumbar plexus nerve that pierces the anterior muscular surface of psoas major, descending before branching into genital and femoral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Genitofemoral nerve: only lumbar plexus nerve piercing and descending on the anterior surface of psoas major.

questions.text: On this gross stomach specimen, identify the notch indicated on the lesser curvature:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Acute notch on the lower part of the lesser curvature demarcating the anatomical boundary between the body and the pyloric antrum.
questions.keyConcept: Incisura angularis: angular notch on the lesser curvature separating the gastric body from the pyloric antrum.

questions.text: In this peritoneal dissection, identify the foramen bounded anteriorly by the lesser omentum:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Peritoneal aperture connecting greater and lesser sacs, bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad.
questions.keyConcept: Epiploic foramen: peritoneal entrance to lesser sac bounded anteriorly by the portal triad in lesser omentum.

questions.text: On this pancreas and duodenum gross specimen, identify the projection passing behind mesenteric vessels:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Medial and inferior hook-like projection of the pancreatic head passing posterior to the superior mesenteric artery and vein.
questions.keyConcept: Uncinate process: lower pancreatic head extension coursing posterior to superior mesenteric artery and vein.

questions.text: On this gross liver specimen, identify the sickle-shaped peritoneal fold indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Two-layered peritoneal fold connecting anterior liver surface to anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, carrying ligamentum teres in free edge.
questions.keyConcept: Falciform ligament: peritoneal fold carrying ligamentum teres hepatis in its inferior free edge.

questions.text: On the posterior surface of this liver specimen, identify the non-peritoneal area indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Non-peritoneal triangular posterior surface directly resting on the diaphragm, bounded by the coronary and triangular ligaments.
questions.keyConcept: Bare area: non-peritoneal posterior hepatic surface bounded by coronary ligaments resting against diaphragm.

questions.text: On the inferior visceral surface of this liver specimen, identify this rectangular lobe:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Rectangular lobe bounded on right by gallbladder fossa, left by fissure for ligamentum teres, and posteriorly by porta hepatis.
questions.keyConcept: Quadrate lobe: visceral hepatic lobe located between gallbladder fossa and fissure for ligamentum teres.

questions.text: In this extrahepatic biliary tree specimen, identify the hepatopancreatic ampulla indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dilation formed by confluence of common bile duct and main pancreatic duct within duodenal wall, discharging at major duodenal papilla.
questions.keyConcept: Ampulla of Vater: hepatopancreatic dilation discharging combined bile and pancreatic juice into duodenum.

questions.text: Examine this small intestinal gross specimen. Which anatomical characteristic distinguishes jejunum from ileum?
options: More abundant mesenteric fat encroaching the bowel wall
More numerous tiers of complex arterial mesenteric arcades
Abundant visible aggregated Peyer's lymphoid nodules
Taller, closely packed plicae circulares and longer vasa recta
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Jejunum possesses wider caliber, thicker wall, prominent plicae circulares, simpler arcades (1–2 tiers), and longer straight vasa recta.
questions.keyConcept: Jejunum characteristics: prominent plicae, simpler arcades with long vasa recta, and less mesenteric fat.

questions.text: On this large bowel specimen, identify these longitudinal outer muscular bands:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Three ribbons of thickened outer longitudinal smooth muscle (free, mesocolic, omental) converging at the root of the vermiform appendix.
questions.keyConcept: Taeniae coli: three longitudinal smooth muscle bands converging at the base of the vermiform appendix.

questions.text: In this coronal section of the anal canal, identify this mucosal boundary line:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Undulating line marking junction of hindgut endoderm and proctodeal ectoderm, dividing visceral innervation/drainage from somatic.
questions.keyConcept: Pectinate line: embryological watershed dividing visceral innervation and drainage from somatic.

questions.text: In this arterial dissection of the abdomen, identify this primary foregut arterial trunk:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Short ventral branch arising from abdominal aorta at T12, giving off left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Celiac trunk: foregut artery arising from aorta at T12 giving left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries.

questions.text: In this stomach arterial arcade dissection, identify this tortuous artery on the pancreas:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Largest celiac branch, characterized by a tortuous course along the superior margin of the pancreas toward the splenic hilum.
questions.keyConcept: Splenic artery: tortuous celiac branch traveling along upper border of pancreas toward spleen and stomach.

questions.text: In this abdominal dissection, identify this midgut artery crossing the 3rd part of the duodenum:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midgut arterial trunk arising at L1, crossing anterior to the uncinate process and 3rd part of the duodenum to enter root of mesentery.
questions.keyConcept: Superior mesenteric artery: midgut arterial supply crossing anterior to the 3rd part of the duodenum.

questions.text: Examine these mesenteric arterial arcades. Identify the small intestinal segment shown:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Multiple overlapping tiers (3 to 5 arcades) with short straight vasa recta and fat-laden mesentery encroaching on the bowel wall.
questions.keyConcept: Ileal arcades: multiple complex tiers (3–5 arcades) with short vasa recta and heavy mesenteric fat.

questions.text: In this transverse mesocolon dissection, identify the colic artery indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: First colic branch of the SMA, ascending between layers of transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon.
questions.keyConcept: Middle colic artery: SMA branch running through transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon.

questions.text: In this lower abdominal dissection, identify this hindgut arterial trunk:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Hindgut trunk arising from aorta at L3, giving left colic and sigmoid branches before continuing as superior rectal artery.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior mesenteric artery: hindgut artery arising at L3 terminating as the superior rectal artery.

questions.text: Behind the neck of the pancreas, identify the venous trunk formed by the union shown:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Large venous trunk formed behind pancreatic neck by confluence of splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein, entering porta hepatis.
questions.keyConcept: Portal vein: formed behind pancreatic neck by the union of splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein.

questions.text: On the inferior aspect of this bony palate, identify the posterolateral foramina indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Posterolateral bilateral foramina piercing the horizontal plates of palatine bones transmitting greater palatine nerve and vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Greater palatine foramina: posterolateral bony palate apertures transmitting neurovascular supply to hard palate.

questions.text: On this bony iliac crest specimen, identify the muscle attaching to the intermediate line:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: The intermediate line of the iliac crest provides origin for the internal oblique (between outer external oblique and inner transversus).
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate line of iliac crest: site of muscular origin for the internal oblique abdominal muscle.

questions.text: On this osteological pelvis specimen, identify the muscle originating from the pubic crest:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Vertical strap muscle arising by two heads from pubic crest and pubic symphysis, ascending within the rectus sheath.
questions.keyConcept: Rectus abdominis: vertical strap muscle arising from pubic crest and symphysis ascending to costal margin.

questions.text: On this typical lumbar vertebra, identify the horizontal posterior process indicated:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Thick, horizontal quadrangular hatchet-shaped process providing attachment for interspinous and supraspinous ligaments.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar spinous process: broad, horizontal hatchet-shaped process providing interspinous ligamentous anchor.

questions.text: On this atypical fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), identify the defining morphological feature:
options: Circular rather than triangular vertebral canal
Massive conical transverse process attached directly to the pedicle and body
Bifid spinous process with posterior hook
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: L5 is characterized by massive conical transverse processes arising directly from both the pedicle and body for the iliolumbar ligament.
questions.keyConcept: L5 vertebra: distinguished by massive conical transverse processes attached directly to the pedicle and body.

questions.text: Examine this clinical photograph. Identify the embryological cause of this anomaly:
options: Failure of fusion between mandibular and lateral nasal prominences
Failure of fusion between lateral palatine processes and nasal septum
Failure of fusion between maxillary and medial nasal prominences
Failure of migration of cranial neural crest cells into 2nd arch
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Unilateral cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the medial nasal prominence (intermaxillary segment).
questions.keyConcept: Cleft lip: developmental failure of fusion between the maxillary prominence and medial nasal prominence.

questions.text: In this diagram of tracheoesophageal anomalies, identify the most common anatomical variant:
options: Proximal tracheoesophageal fistula with distal atresia
Proximal esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Type C (~85% of cases) comprises a blind proximal esophageal pouch and a distal esophageal fistula connecting to the carina.
questions.keyConcept: Tracheoesophageal fistula: Type C (blind upper esophageal pouch with distal fistula) is the most common form.

questions.text: On this axial abdominal CT scan at the transpyloric plane (T12-L1), identify the organ crossing the midline:
questions.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Elongated retroperitoneal parenchymal organ crossing the midline anterior to the aorta, IVC, and superior mesenteric vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Pancreas on axial CT: elongated retroperitoneal organ whose neck crosses anterior to mesenteric vessels at L1.

questions.text: Esophageal manometry in a 35-year-old with dysphagia reveals unrelaxed LES and aperistalsis (achalasia). What is the primary neurogenic defect?
options: Degeneration of inhibitory myenteric neurons producing nitric oxide and VIP
Excessive cholinergic vagal outflow hyperpolarizing esophageal smooth muscle
Loss of sensory afferent fibers in the submucosal Meissner nerve plexus
Autoimmune destruction of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at striated endplates
questions.explanation: Achalasia results from selective degeneration of postganglionic inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus that release nitric oxide (NO) and VIP, preventing lower esophageal sphincter relaxation.
questions.keyConcept: Achalasia: loss of NO/VIP inhibitory myenteric neurons causes aperistalsis and unrelaxed LES.

questions.text: In a lab experiment, introducing acidic chyme (pH < 4.5) into the duodenum triggers copious watery pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate. Which hormone mediates this response?
options: Cholecystokinin (CCK), secreted by mucosal I-cells in response to peptides
Gastrin, released from gastric antral G-cells in response to distension
Motilin, released from upper intestinal M-cells during interdigestive migrating complexes
Secretin, secreted by mucosal S-cells in response to intraluminal hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: Secretin is released by duodenal S-cells when luminal pH drops below 4.5. It acts on pancreatic ductular cells via cAMP to stimulate secretion of large volumes of watery, bicarbonate-rich juice.
questions.keyConcept: Secretin: triggered by duodenal acid -> stimulates ductal aqueous HCO3- secretion.

questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with hepatosplenomegaly, tremor, and Kayser-Fleischer rings (Wilson disease). What is the pathognomonic serum and urine biochemical profile?
options: Elevated serum ceruloplasmin with markedly decreased urinary copper clearance
Markedly elevated serum ferritin, high transferrin saturation, and normal copper
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin, increased free serum copper, and elevated 24-hour urine copper
Deficiency of alpha-1 antitrypsin with normal serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper
questions.explanation: Wilson disease (ATP7B mutation) causes impaired copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin (low ceruloplasmin) and blocked biliary excretion, causing high free serum copper and high urinary copper excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Wilson disease: low serum ceruloplasmin + high urinary copper excretion (ATP7B defect).

questions.text: A 52-year-old female presents with painless jaundice and clay-colored stools. Labs: Total Bilirubin 12 mg/dL, Direct Bilirubin 9.5 mg/dL, and marked elevation of ALP and GGT with mild ALT/AST elevation. What is the diagnosis?
options: Acute viral hepatocellular hepatitis with diffuse hepatic cytolysis
Pre-hepatic hemolytic anemia with predominant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Gilbert syndrome caused by reduced promoter activity of glucuronyl transferase
questions.explanation: Obstructive cholestatic jaundice shows predominant conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia with disproportionate elevation of biliary canalicular enzymes (ALP and GGT) and clay stools from lack of stercobilin.
questions.keyConcept: Cholestatic jaundice: high direct bilirubin + marked elevation of ALP and GGT.

title: Practical — Microbiology
subtitle: Stool Culture, Selective Media & Enteric Pathogens

questions.text: A stool culture on MacConkey agar shows pale non-lactose-fermenting colonies. Subculture on Salmonella-Shigella (SS) agar produces colonies with black centers. Identify the pathogen:
options: Shigella dysenteriae (non-lactose fermenter producing colorless colonies without H2S)
Salmonella enterica (H2S production creates black iron sulfide precipitate)
Escherichia coli (vigorous lactose fermenter producing bright pink dry colonies)
Vibrio cholerae (sucrose fermenter producing bright yellow colonies on TCBS agar)
questions.explanation: On MacConkey agar, Salmonella and Shigella are pale (non-lactose fermenters). On SS agar, Salmonella produces H2S gas which reacts with ferric citrate to produce black-centered colonies.
questions.keyConcept: Salmonella on SS agar = non-lactose fermenting colonies with black H2S centers.

questions.text: Stool from a patient with rice-water diarrhea is cultured on Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose (TCBS) agar, yielding bright yellow colonies. Microscopic examination shows curved Gram-negative rods with darting motility. What is the organism?
options: Vibrio cholerae (sucrose fermentation lowers pH and turns bromothymol blue yellow)
Campylobacter jejuni (microaerophilic thermophilic curved rod growing on Skirrow agar)
Helicobacter pylori (potent urease-producing curved rod colonizing gastric antrum)
Pseudomonas aeruginosa (non-fermenting Gram-negative rod producing green pyocyanin pigment)
questions.explanation: TCBS agar is highly selective and differential for Vibrio. Vibrio cholerae ferments sucrose, producing acid that turns the bromothymol blue pH indicator yellow.
questions.keyConcept: Vibrio cholerae: yellow colonies on TCBS agar + curved Gram-negative rods.

subjects.name: Clinical
lectureNames: Peptic Ulcer Endoscopy & H. pylori Therapy

questions.text: A 45-year-old smoker taking NSAIDs presents with burning epigastric pain 2–3 hours after meals relieved by food. Endoscopy reveals a punched-out duodenal ulcer. What is the essential medical management?
options: Emergency partial gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy reconstruction
High-dose continuous NSAID therapy combined with oral misoprostol monotherapy
Long-term empiric belladonna alkaloid therapy to suppress vagal gastric motility
Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) along with testing and eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers typically cause pain relieved by food and nocturnal pain. Treatment requires profound acid suppression with a PPI and eradication of H. pylori (triple or quadruple regimen).
questions.keyConcept: Duodenal ulcer: epigastric pain relieved by food; treat with PPI + H. pylori eradication.

questions.text: A patient with cirrhosis presents with ascites, splenomegaly, and dilated tortuous superficial periumbilical veins radiating outward (caput medusae). What portosystemic collateral channel produces this sign?
options: Superior vena cava collaterals anastomosing with internal mammary vessels
Left gastric veins anastomosing with lower esophageal tributaries of the azygos vein
Superior rectal vein anastomosing with middle and inferior rectal branches of internal iliac
Recanalized paraumbilical veins communicating with systemic epigastric veins
questions.explanation: Caput medusae results from severe portal hypertension where portal venous blood is shunted through recanalized paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament into superficial and inferior epigastric veins.
questions.keyConcept: Caput medusae = portosystemic shunt through recanalized paraumbilical veins.
